inline_svg <- function(file) {

The experimental `em_*()` functions run e-means one batch at a time, which
lets the data stay on disk while only the current batch visits memory. To
keep things honest, this vignette streams every batch from a binary file of
doubles written with `writeBin()`.

## The data file

Our file holds `n` rows of `d` doubles stored one row after another, and the
last line confirms that its size is exactly what that implies.

```{r}
library(emeans)

set.seed(1)
n <- 20000L
d <- 4L
centers_true <- matrix(c(0, 0, 0, 0,  5, 5, 0, 0,  0, 5, 5, 5), ncol = d, byrow = TRUE)
x <- centers_true[sample(3, n, replace = TRUE), ] + matrix(rnorm(n * d), ncol = d)

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".bin")
con <- file(path, "wb")
writeBin(as.vector(t(x)), con)
close(con)
file.size(path) / (n * d * 8)
```

A small helper fetches any set of rows by seeking to each in turn, which is
slow but perfectly adequate for a demonstration:

```{r}
read_rows <- function(con, rows) {
  out <- matrix(0, length(rows), d)
  for (i in seq_along(rows)) {
    seek(con, (rows[i] - 1) * d * 8)
    out[i, ] <- readBin(con, "double", d)
  }
  out
}
```

## The loop

```{r}
#| echo: false
inline_svg("loop.svg")
```

`em_begin()` takes the total number of rows and the starting centers and
returns a training state, whose `$recipe` holds the two numbers you need to
feed it:

* `recipe$batch_size` rows per batch;
* `recipe$epoch_rows[i]` rows in pass `i`.

The rules come straight from upstream: every batch has exactly `batch_size`
rows except the last of each pass, which takes the remainder, and each pass
delivers exactly `epoch_rows[i]` rows, namely the first that many of a fresh
shuffle of all rows. Each batch goes through `em_accumulate()` and then
`em_update()`, and each pass ends with `em_end_epoch()`; if a batch is too
big to read in one go, you may hand it to `em_accumulate()` in several pieces
that all count towards the same batch.

```{r}
con <- file(path, "rb")
start <- read_rows(con, sample.int(n, 3))
st <- em_begin(n, start, nepochs = 3, threads = 2)
B <- st$recipe$batch_size

labels <- integer(n)
trail <- list(em_centers(st))     # each centroid's position, for the plot below
for (e in seq_along(st$recipe$epoch_rows)) {
  ord <- sample.int(n)[seq_len(st$recipe$epoch_rows[e])]
  for (s in seq(1, length(ord), by = B)) {
    rows <- ord[s:min(s + B - 1, length(ord))]
    stats <- em_accumulate(st, read_rows(con, rows))
    if (!is.null(stats$labels)) {   # only in the last pass
      labels[rows] <- stats$labels
    }
    em_update(st, stats)
    trail[[length(trail) + 1L]] <- em_centers(st)
  }
  em_end_epoch(st)
}
close(con)
fit <- em_finalize(st)
fit
```

`em_finalize()` returns an ordinary `"emeans"` object whose `cluster` is
`NULL`, because only you know where the rows live, so keeping the last-pass
labels falls to you, as in the loop above. `emeans()` would finish with a
sweep that relabels every row against the final centers and adds up the sums
of squares, but the loop has no data left to sweep, so those labels were
computed mid-pass and a few may not match the nearest final center, which
`predict()` will supply on request.

```{r}
round(fit$centers[order(fit$centers[, 1]), ], 1)
table(labels)
```

## Watching the centroids move

The loop also saved `em_centers(st)` after every update, and drawing those
positions on the first two coordinates shows each centroid travelling from
its random start into the middle of its cluster, striding at first and
shuffling by the end as the step size shrinks. Hollow circles mark the random
starts and filled ones the final centers.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| fig-alt: "Grey points from the file, projected on their first two coordinates, with three coloured lines tracing each centroid from its random start into the centre of one of the three clusters, where a large ringed dot marks its final position."
paths <- simplify2array(trail)    # k x d x number of updates
cols <- c("#1F9E80", "#5F6FE0", "#C27A17")
keep <- sample.int(n, 2000)
plot(x[keep, 1:2], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = adjustcolor("#7C7799", alpha.f = 0.3),
     xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2", asp = 1)
for (j in seq_len(nrow(fit$centers))) {
  lines(paths[j, 1, ], paths[j, 2, ], col = cols[j], lwd = 2.5)
  points(paths[j, 1, 1], paths[j, 2, 1], col = cols[j], cex = 1.4, lwd = 2)
}
points(fit$centers[, 1:2], pch = 21, bg = cols, col = "white", cex = 2.4, lwd = 2.5)
points(fit$centers[, 1:2], pch = 1, cex = 3.1, lwd = 1.5)
```

## Checking progress

`em_centers(st)` returns the current centers at any point, which is handy for
keeping an eye on a long run. The functions reject any call that breaks the
batch rules before touching the state, so a failed call costs nothing and can
be retried with the right rows.

```{r}
#| include: false
unlink(path)
```

For data that fits in memory, `emeans()` runs this very loop for you and
spares you the bookkeeping.
